name: GRACE
seoDesc: GRACE: work out your result from the age and the pulse. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The answer is what the GRACE calculator works out, and it gets there from the age, the pulse, the systolic BP and the creatinine. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis.

The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the GRACE calculator work?
sections.html:
The GRACE calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the killip class); then you type in the age, the pulse, the systolic BP and the creatinine.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in years.
  • A number, expressed in bpm.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters of mercury. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as I (no signs of CHF), II (rales, elevated JVP) and III (pulmonary edema). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Segment ST deviation”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A number, expressed in pts.
  • A number, expressed in pts.

4 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the GRACE calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Enzymes=-39 ÷ 14 × cardiac Arrest + (1 ÷ 14) × in-hospital − 1 ÷ 14 × killip class − 2 × segment ST − 1 ÷ 14 × (age) − 1 ÷ 14 × (creatinine) − 1 ÷ 14 × (pulse) − 1 ÷ 14 × (systolic BP)
Enzymes=-30 ÷ 13 × cardiac Arrest + (1 ÷ 13) × within 6 months from admission − 17 ÷ 13 × segment ST − 1 ÷ 13 × (age) − 1 ÷ 13 × (creatinine) − 1 ÷ 13 × (pulse) − 1 ÷ 13 × (killip class) − 1 ÷ 13 × (systolic BP)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Creatinine, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The GRACE calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the pulse and the systolic BP — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the GRACE calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the pulse, the systolic BP and the creatinine, which is 8 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter systolic BP in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Systolic BP opens in millimeters of mercury and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the GRACE calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
